title: Sequences & Progressions
summary: Progressions are lists that follow a fixed rule: APs add a constant, GPs multiply by one, HPs hide an AP in their reciprocals, and special series come with ready-made sum formulas. Alongside term-pattern sequences, this block gives a quick mark in SSC, Railway and Banking papers and anchors the series questions of CAT algebra.

subtopics.title: Arithmetic Progressions
subtopics.concept: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers that grows or falls by the same fixed amount, the common difference $d$. Its $n$-th term is $a + (n-1)d$, and its $n$-term sum is $\dfrac{n}{2}$ times (first + last). Row-of-seats, monthly savings and wage-step questions are APs in disguise.

formulas.name: nth term
formulas.note: $a$ is the first term, $d$ the common difference.

formulas.name: Middle term
formulas.note: Only when the count $n$ is odd.

tricks.title: The middle term is the average
tricks.body: For an odd count of AP terms, sum $=$ middle $\times$ count. One division gives the middle term, and one multiplication gives the sum.

example.q: The sum of 9 terms of an AP is 135. Its middle term is:

tricks.title: Equidistant terms add to the same value
tricks.body: $a_2 + a_{15}$, $a_1 + a_{16}$ — pairs placed equally far from the ends share one sum. A sum of all $n$ terms then needs no $a$ or $d$ at all.

example.q: In an AP of 16 terms, the sum of the 2nd and 15th terms is 40. Find the sum of all 16 terms.

tricks.title: Name three terms a-d, a, a+d
tricks.body: Three consecutive AP terms collapse to one unknown $a$ plus $d$. Sum gives $a$ at once; product or another condition then gives $d$.

example.q: The sum of three numbers in AP is 27 and their product is 504. Find the numbers.

mistakes: Using $a + nd$ for the nth term — the 1st term must come out at $n = 1$, so the term is $a + (n-1)d$.
Writing the sum as $\dfrac{n}{2} \times$ last term — the rule is $\dfrac{n}{2} \times$ (first term + last term).
Using $(b - a)/k$ as the gap when inserting $k$ arithmetic means — the $k$ means create $k + 1$ steps, so the gap is $(b-a)/(k+1)$.
In word problems, taking the 10th row as $a + 10d$ — row 1 is $a$ itself, so row 10 is $a + 9d$.
Forgetting that an AP may have a negative common difference — terms then fall, and the sum can shrink as $n$ grows.
Looking for a middle term when the count is even — no single middle term exists, so the $S_n/n$ shortcut does not apply.
subtopics.notes:
### What an arithmetic progression is
An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers with one simple rule. Every term comes from the previous term by adding the same fixed number.

That fixed number is the **common difference**, written $d$. The first term is $a$.

Seats in a hall: row 1 has 12 seats, row 2 has 15, row 3 has 18. Here $a = 12$ and $d = 3$.

> **Rule:** Before using any formula, check $d$. Subtract any two neighbouring terms — the answer must be the same everywhere.

A falling list like 40, 36, 32 is also an AP. Its $d$ is $-4$. A difference can be zero, positive or negative.

### The nth term
The $n$-th term is the first term plus $n - 1$ jumps of size $d$.

$$a_n = a + (n - 1)d$$

Why $n - 1$? From term 1 to term 10 there are 9 jumps, not 10.

The 10th term of 7, 11, 15, ... is $7 + 9 \times 4 = 43$.

The last of $n$ terms is $a + (n-1)d$ — the same formula counted from the other end.

> **Tip:** In word problems, "the 10th row" means $n = 10$. The 10th row is $a + 9d$, never $a + 10d$.

### The sum of n terms
Add the first and the last term. An AP makes every such pair equal: $a_1 + a_n = a_2 + a_{n-1}$, and so on.

There are $n$ such pairs, shared between two terms at a time. Half of $n$ pairs, each worth first + last:

$$S_n = \frac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right] \qquad S_n = \frac{n}{2}(\text{first} + \text{last})$$

Sum of 20 terms of 5, 9, 13, ...: $\dfrac{20}{2}[10 + 19 \times 4] = 10 \times 86 = 860$.

### The middle term trick
For an odd number of terms, the middle term equals the average.

$$\text{middle} = \frac{S_n}{n}$$

The sum of 15 terms is 375, so the 8th (middle) term is $\dfrac{375}{15} = 25$.

Three consecutive terms are best named $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$. Their sum is $3a$, so $a$ is the sum divided by 3.

The sum of three numbers in AP is 27 and their product is 504. Middle $= 9$, so $9(81 - d^2) = 504$, giving $d = 5$: the numbers are 4, 9, 14.

> **Example:** Terms equally far from the ends add to the same value: $a_2 + a_{15} = a_1 + a_{16}$.

### Inserting arithmetic means
Numbers placed between two numbers so that the whole list becomes an AP are arithmetic means (AMs).

With $k$ means between $a$ and $b$, the $k$ means create $k + 1$ equal jumps:

$$d = \frac{b - a}{k + 1}$$

Insert 4 means between 8 and 23: $d = \dfrac{15}{5} = 3$, so the means are 11, 14, 17, 20.

> **Watch:** Divide by $k + 1$, not by $k$. Four means between two numbers make five gaps.

### Word problems: rows, savings, wages
Translate the story into $a$, $d$ and $n$ first.

- First month or first row gives $a$.
- The fixed increase every step gives $d$.
- A total asks for $S_n$; the value of step $n$ is $a + (n-1)d$.

A man saves Rs 200 in the first month and adds Rs 25 every month. Twelve months: $S_{12} = \dfrac{12}{2}[400 + 11 \times 25] = 6 \times 675 = 4050$.

Seats: 15 rows, first row 15 chairs, each row 2 more. Last row $= 15 + 14 \times 2 = 43$; total $= \dfrac{15}{2}(15 + 43) = 435$.

> **Tip:** Say what each symbol means in the story before touching the formulas.

patterns.name: nth term of an AP
patterns.howToSpot: A list with a constant gap is given, and a specific term (5th, 10th, last) is asked.
patterns.why: Each step of the list adds exactly one $d$, and reaching term $n$ takes $n - 1$ steps.

example.q: Find the 10th term of the AP 7, 11, 15, 19, ...

patterns.name: Sum of n terms of an AP
patterns.howToSpot: 'Find the sum of the first 20 terms' — a total of a constant-gap list is asked.
patterns.why: Equal end-pairs let the whole sum collapse to (average term) × (number of terms).

example.q: Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 5, 9, 13, ...

patterns.name: Which term of the AP is this value?
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which term of 3, 8, 13, ... is 78?' — a value is given and its position $n$ is asked.
patterns.why: The target value fixes the number of $d$-jumps after the first term.

example.q: Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, 18, ... is 78?

patterns.name: Middle term: sum, average and three-term problems
patterns.howToSpot: The sum of an odd number of AP terms is given and the middle term is asked — or three AP numbers hide behind a sum and a product.
steps: Divide the sum by the count for the middle term.
Use the product (or second condition) to find $d$.
patterns.why: In an AP the average sits exactly at the middle, and three consecutive terms are symmetric about it.

example.q: The sum of 15 terms of an AP is 375. Find the 8th term.

patterns.name: Insert arithmetic means between a and b
patterns.howToSpot: 'Insert 4 arithmetic means between 8 and 23' — the means, their gap, or one of them is asked.
patterns.why: The $k$ inserted numbers split the distance from $a$ to $b$ into $k + 1$ equal jumps.

patterns.name: AP word problems: rows, seats, savings, wages
patterns.howToSpot: Seats grow by a fixed number per row, savings by a fixed amount per month, wages by a fixed step — a total or a later value is asked.
patterns.why: A story with a constant per-step change is exactly an AP wearing words.

example.q: A hall has 18 rows of chairs; the first row has 15 chairs and each row has 3 more than the previous row. How many chairs are there in all?

revision: nth term: $a + (n-1)d$ — $n-1$ jumps, not $n$.
Sum: $\dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$ or $\dfrac{n}{2}(\text{first} + \text{last})$.
Middle term of an odd-count AP $= S_n \div n$.
Terms equidistant from the ends add to the same value.
Inserting $k$ means: gap $= \dfrac{b-a}{k+1}$.
Three AP terms: $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$; their sum is $3a$.

subtopics.title: Geometric Progressions
subtopics.concept: A geometric progression (GP) grows or shrinks by a fixed multiplier, the common ratio $r$. Its $n$-th term is $ar^{n-1}$, and a GP with $|r| < 1$ has an infinite sum of $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$. Doubling money, bounce heights and repeated percentage growth are GPs in disguise.

formulas.name: nth term
formulas.note: $r$ is the common ratio; power is $n-1$.

formulas.name: Bouncing ball total
formulas.note: $h$ is the drop height, $r$ the rebound fraction.

tricks.title: Name three GP terms a/r, a, ar
tricks.body: The product of the three is $a^3$, so a given product fixes the middle term at once. The sum then fixes $r$.

example.q: Three numbers in GP have sum 21 and product 216. Find them.

tricks.title: Sum to infinity reflex
tricks.body: See an endless list whose ratio sits between $-1$ and 1 — divide the first term by ($1 - r$). One division, no powers.

tricks.title: Bouncing ball: first drop once, pairs twice
tricks.body: Add the first drop, then twice the sum of all rebounds. The rebound chain is a GP with first term $hr$.

example.q: A ball is dropped from 36 m and rebounds to half its height each time. Find the total distance travelled.

mistakes: Using $a r^n$ for the nth term — at $n = 1$ it must give $a$, so the term is $a r^{n-1}$.
Applying $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$ to every GP — it works only when $|r| < 1$; for $r = 2$ the sum simply grows.
Mixing signs: $\dfrac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$ and $\dfrac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$ are the same sum; flipping one sign makes it negative.
Counting the first drop twice in a bouncing-ball question — the first fall happens once; later up-and-down pairs happen twice.
Treating 'doubles every year' as an AP — doubling is a GP with $r = 2$.
Forgetting the $r = 1$ case — a GP with $r = 1$ is a constant list, and its sum is $n \times a$.
subtopics.notes:
### What a geometric progression is
A geometric progression (GP) is a list where every term comes from the previous one by multiplying the same fixed number.

That number is the **common ratio**, written $r$. The first term is $a$.

3, 6, 12, 24 is a GP: each term is twice the one before. Here $a = 3$ and $r = 2$.

Doubling money, bounce heights and repeated percentage growth all move by a fixed ratio.

> **Rule:** Check $r$ first: divide any term by the one before it. The answer must be the same everywhere.

A ratio can be a fraction. 8, 4, 2, 1 has $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$ — the list shrinks toward zero.

### The nth term
The $n$-th term is the first term multiplied by $n - 1$ jumps of the ratio.

$$a_n = a r^{\,n-1}$$

The 5th term of 3, 6, 12, ... is $3 \times 2^4 = 48$.

> **Tip:** The power is one less than the term number. Term 5 uses $2^4$, because term 1 uses $2^0$.

### The sum of n terms
Multiply the first term by ($r^n - 1$), then divide by ($r - 1$):

$$S_n = \frac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}, \qquad r \ne 1$$

Sum of 6 terms of 4, 12, 36, ...: $\dfrac{4(3^6 - 1)}{2} = 2 \times 728 = 1456$.

If $r = 1$, every term equals $a$, and the sum is simply $n \times a$.

> **Watch:** $\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$ and $\dfrac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}$ are the same sum. Keep the signs consistent.

### Sum to infinity
When $r$ lies between $-1$ and 1, the terms shrink and the total settles at one number.

$$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r}, \qquad |r| < 1$$

$8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + \cdots$: $a = 8$, $r = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so the sum is $\dfrac{8}{1/2} = 16$.

> **Watch:** This formula fails for $r = 2$ or any ratio of size 1 or more. The list must shrink.

### Three-term tricks
Three consecutive GP terms are best named $\dfrac{a}{r}$, $a$, $ar$. Their product is $a^3$.

Three numbers in GP have sum 21 and product 216. Then $a^3 = 216$, so $a = 6$. Now $\dfrac{6}{r} + 6 + 6r = 21$ gives $r = 2$: the numbers are 3, 6, 12.

The middle of any three terms is the geometric mean of its neighbours: $b^2 = ac$.

### Bounces and doubling
A ball dropped from height $h$, rebounding to a fraction $r$ each time, travels in total:

$$h + \frac{2hr}{1 - r}$$

The first drop happens once; every later up-and-down pair happens twice.

From 36 m, rebounding to half each time: the rebounds are $18 + 9 + 4.5 + \cdots = 36$. Total $= 36 + 2 \times 36 = 108$ m.

Money that multiplies is a GP too. Savings of Rs 2, 4, 8, ... for 10 months total $2(2^{10} - 1) = 2046$.

Rs 1 doubled daily for 15 days gives $1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots + 2^{14} = 2^{15} - 1 = 32767$.

> **Tip:** "Doubles every year or hour" means $r = 2$. "Grows 10% every year" means $r = 1.1$ — a GP, not an AP.

patterns.why: Each step multiplies by $r$, and reaching term $n$ takes $n - 1$ multiplications.

patterns.howToSpot: 'Sum of the first 6 terms' of a multiplying list, or 'how many terms give total S'.
patterns.why: Subtracting $rS_n$ from $S_n$ collapses the list, which gives the closed form.

patterns.name: Sum to infinity
patterns.howToSpot: An endless list with $|r| < 1$ (8 + 4 + 2 + ...) and its total is asked — or the total and one of $a$, $r$ are given.
steps: Reverse use: find $a$ or $r$ from the given sum.
patterns.why: As $n$ grows, $r^n$ vanishes for $|r| < 1$, so the finite sum settles at $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.

example.q: Find the sum of the infinite GP 9 + 3 + 1 + 1/3 + ...

patterns.name: Three numbers in GP (sum and product given)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Three numbers in GP' with their sum and product — the numbers are asked.
patterns.why: The symmetric naming makes the product collapse to $a^3$ and the sum linear in $r$.

example.q: Three numbers in GP have sum 21 and product 216. Find the numbers.

patterns.name: Bouncing ball and repeating distances
patterns.howToSpot: A ball or pendulum covers a fixed fraction of its previous path each time; the total distance is asked.
steps: Each later up-down pair: twice the rebound chain.
Rebound chain is a GP; sum it for $|r| < 1$.
patterns.why: After the first fall, every stretch is travelled twice, and the stretch sizes form a GP.

example.q: A ball is dropped from 36 m and rebounds to half its height each time. Find the total distance.

patterns.name: Doubling money and repeated growth
patterns.howToSpot: Savings double each month, a count doubles each hour, or a value grows by a fixed per cent each period.
patterns.why: Any fixed multiplier per period makes the list a GP, so both formulas apply.

example.q: A man saves Rs 2 in the first month, Rs 4 in the second, Rs 8 in the third, and so on. Find his total savings in 10 months.

revision: nth term: $ar^{n-1}$.
Sum of $n$ terms: $\dfrac{a(r^n-1)}{r-1}$; if $r = 1$, it is $na$.
Sum to infinity: $\dfrac{a}{1-r}$, only for $|r| < 1$.
Three GP terms $\dfrac{a}{r}, a, ar$; product $= a^3$.
Ball: total $= h + \dfrac{2hr}{1-r}$.
'Doubles' means $r = 2$; '+10% per period' means $r = 1.1$.

subtopics.title: Harmonic Progressions & AGP
subtopics.concept: A harmonic progression (HP) is a list whose reciprocals form an AP, so every HP question is solved on the reciprocals. Two related tools sit beside it: the AM-GM-HM trio for two positive numbers, and the arithmetico-geometric series, where an AP and a GP are multiplied term by term.

formulas.name: nth term of an HP
formulas.note: $a$, $d$ come from the AP of reciprocals.

formulas.name: HM of two numbers
formulas.note: The reciprocal of the AM of the reciprocals.

formulas.name: AM x HM = GM squared
formulas.note: For positive numbers, AM $\ge$ GM $\ge$ HM.

tricks.title: Flip every HP into its AP
tricks.body: Reciprocal the list, do all the work with AP tools, reciprocal the final answer. This solves every HP question.

example.q: Which term of the HP 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... is 1/32?

tricks.title: AM x HM = GM squared
tricks.body: One relation replaces a page of algebra. Any two of AM, GM, HM give the third.

example.q: The AM of two numbers is 10 and their GM is 8. Find the HM.

tricks.title: AGP: multiply by r and subtract
tricks.body: Write $rS$ below $S$ with the powers aligned. Subtracting kills the middle and leaves a small GP minus one end.

steps: Line up $S$ and $2S$ with equal powers of 2.

mistakes: Looking for a common difference in an HP — the HP terms have none; their reciprocals do.
Writing the HP nth term as $\dfrac{1}{a} + (n-1)\dfrac{1}{d}$ — the whole denominator changes: $\dfrac{1}{a + (n-1)d}$.
Using the infinite AGP sum without checking $|r| < 1$ — the formula fails for $r = 2$ or larger.
Writing AM $\le$ GM $\le$ HM — for positive numbers the order is AM $\ge$ GM $\ge$ HM.
Subtracting the shifted AGP series with powers out of line — align matching powers before subtracting.
Reporting an HM larger than the AM — that is impossible for positive numbers, so recheck the working.
subtopics.notes:
### What a harmonic progression is
A harmonic progression (HP) is a list whose reciprocals form an AP.

1/2, 1/5, 1/8, 1/11 is an HP. Turn it upside down: 2, 5, 8, 11 — an AP with $a = 2$ and $d = 3$.

The HP terms themselves have no common difference. Never look for one.

> **Rule:** Every HP question is solved on the reciprocals. Flip first, work in the AP, flip back at the end.

### Working with an HP
The $n$-th term of the HP is the reciprocal of the AP's $n$-th term:

$$a_n = \frac{1}{a + (n-1)d}$$

Here $a$ and $d$ belong to the AP of reciprocals.

Which term of 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... is 1/32? Solve $2 + (n-1)3 = 32$, so $n = 11$: the 11th term.

Which term of 1/5, 1/8, 1/11, ... is 1/29? Solve $5 + (n-1)3 = 29$, so $n = 9$.

Given two HP terms, write the two reciprocals as AP terms. If the 4th term is 1/10 and the 10th is 1/28, then $a_4 = 10$ and $a_{10} = 28$, so $d = 3$ and $a = 1$. The 15th HP term is $\dfrac{1}{1 + 14 \times 3} = \dfrac{1}{43}$.

> **Tip:** In $\dfrac{1}{a + (n-1)d}$ the whole expression sits under the 1. Writing $\dfrac{1}{a} + (n-1)\dfrac{1}{d}$ is a different list.

### The AM-GM-HM trio
For two positive numbers $x$ and $y$: AM $= \dfrac{x+y}{2}$, GM $= \sqrt{xy}$, HM $= \dfrac{2xy}{x+y}$.

They always line up in the order AM $\ge$ GM $\ge$ HM.

The three are tied by one clean relation:

$$AM \times HM = GM^2$$

The AM of two numbers is 10 and the GM is 8, so the HM is $\dfrac{64}{10} = 6.4$.

The relation also finds the numbers. AM is 13 and GM is 12: sum 26, product 144, so the numbers are 8 and 18.

> **Note:** For two numbers, the HM is the reciprocal of the AM of the reciprocals — the HP idea again.

### What an AGP looks like
An arithmetico-geometric series (AGP) multiplies two patterns: the coefficients grow by addition, the powers grow by multiplication.

$$1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 8 + 5 \cdot 16$$

The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 form an AP; the powers of 2 form a GP. Neither plain sum formula works.

### The AGP subtraction method
Multiply the whole series by $r$ and write it below $S$, with equal powers lined up. Subtract.

For $S = 1 + 2 \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 8 + 5 \cdot 16 = 129$:

$S - 2S = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 - 160 = -129$, so $S = 129$.

The coefficients drop by one, leaving a small GP minus one far end. That leftover sum is easy.

> **Tip:** Line up the powers before subtracting. A misaligned shift is the classic error here.

### Infinite AGP sums
When $|r| < 1$, the finite method settles into a formula. For $a + (a+d)r + (a+2d)r^2 + \cdots$:

$$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r} + \frac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$$

$1 + \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{3}{9} + \dfrac{4}{27} + \cdots$: here $a = 1$, $d = 1$, $r = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Sum $= \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{1/3}{4/9} = \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{9}{4}$.

> **Watch:** The formula needs $|r| < 1$. For $r = 2$ the terms grow and no sum exists.

patterns.name: Which term of an HP is it?
patterns.howToSpot: A fraction list like 1/2, 1/5, 1/8 is given and the position of one term is asked.
steps: Flip the list into its AP.
patterns.why: The reciprocals are an AP, so position questions become ordinary AP equations.

example.q: Which term of the HP 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... is 1/32?

patterns.name: Find an HP term from two given HP terms
patterns.howToSpot: Two terms of an HP are given (say the 4th and the 10th) and another term is asked.
steps: Write the two reciprocals as AP terms.
Compute the AP term and flip it back.
patterns.why: Two AP terms fix $a$ and $d$, and every other term follows from them.

example.q: The 4th term of an HP is 1/10 and the 10th term is 1/28. Find the 15th term.

patterns.name: AM, GM, HM of two numbers
patterns.howToSpot: AM, GM or HM of two positive numbers is given (two of them), and the third — or the numbers — are asked.
steps: Use $AM \times HM = GM^2$ for the missing average.
AM gives the sum; GM gives the product.
Solve the quadratic for the two numbers.
patterns.why: AM fixes the sum, GM fixes the product, and two numbers with a given sum and product are unique up to order.

example.q: The AM of two positive numbers is 13 and their GM is 12. Find the numbers.

patterns.name: AGP: finite sum by subtraction
patterns.howToSpot: Terms like 1 + 2·2 + 3·4 + 4·8 — a counting part times a powering part.
steps: Sum the leftover small GP and solve for $S$.
patterns.why: The shift by one power turns each AGP term into a single GP term plus a constant.

patterns.name: Infinite AGP sum
patterns.howToSpot: An endless AGP like 1 + 2/3 + 3/9 + 4/27 + ... with $|r| < 1$.
patterns.why: As the powers die out, the subtraction method leaves exactly $\dfrac{a}{1-r} + \dfrac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$.

revision: HP: reciprocals form an AP — always flip first.
HP nth term: $\dfrac{1}{a + (n-1)d}$.
AM $\times$ HM $=$ GM$^2$; AM $\ge$ GM $\ge$ HM.
HM of $a, b$: $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$.
AGP: multiply $S$ by $r$, align, subtract.
Infinite AGP: $\dfrac{a}{1-r} + \dfrac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$ for $|r| < 1$.

subtopics.title: Special Series & Standard Sums
subtopics.concept: Some sums are so common that formulas exist: $\sum n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\sum n^2 = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$, $\sum n^3 = \left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$. Telescoping fractions cancel in a line, leaving only the ends. One formula pick usually finishes the question.

formulas.name: Sum of first n cubes
formulas.note: The square of the natural-number sum.

tricks.title: Pair the ends of a natural-number sum
tricks.body: 1 + 40, 2 + 39, ... every pair adds to 41. With 20 pairs, the sum is $20 \times 41$. The formula $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ does the same in one line.

tricks.title: Odd numbers build squares
tricks.body: Count the odd numbers; the sum is that count squared. A run that starts past 1 is a difference of two squares.

tricks.title: Telescoping: keep only the ends
tricks.body: Split each fraction as a difference. Writing the first few terms shows the middle cancelling in a diagonal line.

mistakes: Using $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ for squares or cubes — each power has its own formula.
Forgetting to square $\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]$ in the sum of cubes.
Counting terms as $b - a$ — from $a$ to $b$ inclusive there are $b - a + 1$ terms.
Squaring the count for odd numbers that do not start at 1 — $11 + 13 + \cdots + 29$ is $15^2 - 5^2$, not $10^2$.
Adding telescoping fractions one by one — pair the cancellations; only the two ends survive.
subtopics.notes:
### Three power sums
Three formulas cover most direct asks. For the first $n$ natural numbers:

$$\sum n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \qquad \sum n^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \qquad \sum n^3 = \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$$

$1 + 2 + \cdots + 40 = \dfrac{40 \times 41}{2} = 820$.

$1^2 + 2^2 + \cdots + 10^2 = \dfrac{10 \times 11 \times 21}{6} = 385$.

$1^3 + 2^3 + \cdots + 5^3 = \left(\dfrac{5 \times 6}{2}\right)^2 = 15^2 = 225$.

> **Rule:** The cube sum is the square of the natural-number sum. Memorise all three shapes.

### Odd and even number sums
The first $n$ odd numbers add to a perfect square:

$$1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + (2n-1) = n^2$$

$1 + 3 + \cdots + 25$ has 13 odd numbers, so the sum is $13^2 = 169$.

The first $n$ even numbers add to $n(n+1)$: $2 + 4 + \cdots + 20 = 10 \times 11 = 110$.

An odd-number run that starts later is the difference of two squares. $11 + 13 + \cdots + 29 = 15^2 - 5^2 = 200$, because 11 is the 6th odd number and 29 the 15th.

> **Tip:** $n^2$ works only when the run starts at 1. Otherwise subtract two square sums.

### Count the terms first
From $a$ to $b$, both included, the count is $b - a + 1$.

$21 + 22 + \cdots + 50 = \dfrac{50 \times 51}{2} - \dfrac{20 \times 21}{2} = 1275 - 210 = 1065$.

Subtracting the sum up to 20 removes the first 20 terms cleanly.

> **Watch:** 21 to 50 is 30 terms, not 29. The $+1$ matters.

### Telescoping sums
A telescoping sum hides cancellations. Each fraction splits into two parts:

$$\frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}$$

So $\dfrac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \dfrac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{9 \cdot 10} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{9}{10}$.

Everything in the middle cancels. Only the first and last pieces survive.

The gaps need not be 1. $\dfrac{1}{1 \cdot 5} + \dfrac{1}{5 \cdot 9} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{37 \cdot 41} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{41}\right) = \dfrac{10}{41}$.

> **Rule:** Split each term as a difference of two simple fractions, then cancel in one line.

### Sums of consecutive products
$1 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 + \cdots + n(n+1)$ has a ready answer:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} k(k+1) = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}$$

Up to $10 \times 11$: $\dfrac{10 \times 11 \times 12}{3} = 440$.

In reverse, a total of 168 means $n(n+1)(n+2) = 504 = 7 \times 8 \times 9$, so $n = 7$.

> **Note:** The formula comes from $k(k+1) = \dfrac{k^3 - k}{3}$ plus the power sums.

### Choosing the formula
Read the question, name the last term, then pick:

- A plain list of numbers gives $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, or a difference of two such sums.
- Squares, cubes or products point to the matching formula above.
- A chain of fractions points to telescoping.

A sum like $2^2 + 4^2 + \cdots + 20^2$ is $4(1^2 + \cdots + 10^2) = 4 \times 385 = 1540$.

> **Tip:** Factor out the common piece first; the power sum then applies to small numbers.

patterns.name: Sum of a run of natural numbers
patterns.howToSpot: A run like 21 + 22 + ... + 50, or a reverse ask: 'the sum 1 to n is S, find n'.
steps: Find the count: last minus first plus 1.
Subtract the part before the start.
patterns.why: A run from $a$ to $b$ is (sum up to $b$) minus (sum up to $a - 1$).

patterns.name: Sum of squares
patterns.howToSpot: A list of squares 1² + 2² + ... + n², sometimes with a factor like even squares only.
steps: Factor out common pieces first for even or odd squares.
patterns.why: The closed form replaces adding every square individually — one formula, no listing.

patterns.name: Sum of cubes
patterns.howToSpot: 1³ + 2³ + ... appears, or a cube sum equals a square in disguise.
patterns.why: The cube sum equals the square of the triangular number — the fastest cube fact in exams.

patterns.name: Sum of odd and even numbers
patterns.howToSpot: Runs of odd or even numbers, starting at 1 (or 2) or later.
steps: Count the terms in the run.
Start at 1: the sum is the count squared.
Start later: subtract two square sums.
patterns.why: Each new odd number extends the previous square by one L-shaped layer, so $n$ odds make $n^2$.

patterns.name: Telescoping fraction sums
patterns.howToSpot: A fraction chain with overlapping denominators: 1/(1·2) + 1/(2·3) + ..., or gaps of more than 1.
steps: Split each term into a difference.
Keep the first piece of term 1 and the last piece of the final term.
patterns.why: Each split term cancels most of the next one, so the whole chain collapses to its two ends.

patterns.name: Sums of consecutive products
patterns.howToSpot: 1×2 + 2×3 + 3×4 + ... — neighbouring whole numbers multiply.
steps: Reverse asks: match the total with three consecutive numbers.
patterns.why: The product chain equals one third of $n(n+1)(n+2)$, so both directions are one line.

revision: $\sum n = \dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\sum n^2 = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$, $\sum n^3 = \left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$.
First $n$ odd numbers: $n^2$; first $n$ even numbers: $n(n+1)$.
Run from $a$ to $b$: subtract two power sums; count is $b - a + 1$.
Telescoping: $\dfrac{1}{k(k+1)} = \dfrac{1}{k} - \dfrac{1}{k+1}$; only the ends survive.
$1 \times 2 + \cdots + n(n+1) = \dfrac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{3}$.
Factor common pieces (like $2^2$) before applying a power sum.

subtopics.title: Pattern Sequences: Next, Missing & Wrong Terms
subtopics.concept: A pattern sequence hides a rule, and the question asks for the next term, a missing term, or the wrong term. The work is a fixed routine: take differences, check ratios, split alternating chains, and test position rules like $n^2$ or $2^n$.

formulas.name: Common position rules
formulas.note: Compare each term with its position $n$.

formulas.name: Multiply-and-add rule
formulas.note: A frequent hidden rule; test it when differences fail.

tricks.title: Take differences, then differences again
tricks.body: The first differences often hide a second pattern — odd numbers, squares, doubling. Two ladders solve most series.

tricks.title: Split alternating series into two chains
tricks.body: One rule for odd positions, one for even positions. Answer from the chain the asked position belongs to.

tricks.title: Test the position rules
tricks.body: Compare each term with $n^2$, $n^3$, $n^2 \pm 1$, $2^n$ and primes at its position. One of them usually snaps into place.

mistakes: Testing only addition — many series multiply, alternate two operations, or follow squares and cubes.
Stopping at the first difference — the differences themselves often form a pattern (second differences).
Applying one chain's rule to the other in an alternating series — split the series first.
Ignoring the position of each term — rules like $n^2 + 1$ tie a term to its place in the list.
Changing two things at once while testing a guessed rule — a valid rule must fit every given term unchanged.
subtopics.notes:
### What a pattern sequence asks
A list of numbers hides a rule. The question asks for the next term, a missing middle term, or the one wrong term.

There is no formula to memorise. There is a routine: test the common rules in order until one fits every term.

> **Rule:** A correct rule must match every given term. Two matching terms prove nothing.

### The difference ladder
Subtract each term from the next. If the differences are equal, it is an AP — add the difference once more.

If the differences differ, take their differences too (the second differences).

2, 5, 10, 17, 26: the gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9 — the odd numbers. Next gap is 11, so the next term is $26 + 11 = 37$.

The same list is $n^2 + 1$: $1^2+1$, $2^2+1$, $3^2+1$, ... Both roads give 37.

3, 4, 8, 17, 33: gaps are 1, 4, 9, 16 — the squares. Next gap 25 gives 58.

> **Tip:** Odd-number gaps, square gaps and doubling gaps cover most exam series.

### Multiply and mixed operations
When the list grows fast, try division instead of subtraction.

5, 10, 20, 40: each term is double the one before, so the next is 80.

2, 4, 12, 48, 240: the multipliers are $\times 2$, $\times 3$, $\times 4$, $\times 5$, so the next multiplier is 6 and the next term is 1440.

Mixed rules multiply and add: 5, 11, 23, 47 uses "$\times 2 + 1$" each time, giving 95 next.

> **Watch:** A ratio check (divide neighbours) catches multiplication; a difference check cannot.

### Two alternating chains
Odd-position terms and even-position terms can follow different rules.

5, 9, 7, 11, 9, 13: positions 1, 3, 5 give 5, 7, 9 ($+2$). Positions 2, 4, 6 give 9, 11, 13 ($+2$). The 7th term belongs to the first chain: 11.

7, 12, 10, 15, 13, 18: chains $7, 10, 13$ and $12, 15, 18$, both $+3$. Next is 16.

> **Tip:** If one single rule fails after two or three terms, split odd and even positions before anything else.

### Position-based rules
Many series tie each term to its position $n$:

- $n^2$: 1, 4, 9, 16.
- $n^3$: 1, 8, 27, 64.
- $n^2 - 1$: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35.
- $n^n$: 1, 4, 27, 256.

3, 8, 15, 24, 35: these are $2^2-1$, $3^2-1$, $4^2-1$, ..., so the next is $7^2 - 1 = 48$.

Prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and their $\pm 1$ shifts appear often too.

### Missing and wrong terms
A missing middle term uses the same routine — the rule must fit both neighbours.

7, 14, 28, ?, 112: each term doubles, so the missing term is 56.

2, 3, 6, ?, 14, 15, 30: the rule alternates $+1$ and $\times 2$, so the missing term is 7.

For a wrong-number question, build the correct series from the rule, then point at the term that breaks it.

2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 40, 56: the rule is $n(n+1)$, so the sixth term should be 42. The wrong number is 40.

> **Example:** 5, 11, 23, 47, 94, 191 — the rule "$\times 2 + 1$" gives 95 in fifth place, so 94 is wrong.

patterns.name: Next term by the difference ladder
patterns.howToSpot: A plain list of growing numbers; the gaps themselves show a pattern.
steps: If needed, write the second differences.
Extend the gap pattern and add.
patterns.why: Differences strip one layer of the rule, and the layer beneath is usually a familiar list.

patterns.name: Next term by multiply or divide
patterns.howToSpot: The list grows (or shrinks) fast; dividing neighbours gives equal or stepping ratios.
steps: Divide each term by the one before.
patterns.why: Constant or stepping multipliers show up only under division, never under subtraction.

patterns.name: Two alternating chains
patterns.howToSpot: The numbers jump up and down, or one clean rule fits only every other term.
steps: Split into odd and even positions.
Answer from the chain that owns the asked position.
patterns.why: Two interleaved simple rules look like chaos until the positions are separated.

patterns.name: Squares, cubes and position rules
patterns.howToSpot: The terms sit near familiar squares or cubes — one less, one more, or the cubes themselves.
steps: Apply the rule at the next position.
patterns.why: Offset squares and cubes are the most reused hidden rules in exam series.

patterns.name: Missing term inside the series
patterns.howToSpot: A '?' sits between two given terms instead of at the end.
steps: Find a rule that fits every known term.
Apply it at the missing position.
Check the answer against both neighbours.
patterns.why: A middle term must satisfy the rule from both sides, which makes it a strong check.

patterns.name: Wrong number in the series
patterns.howToSpot: 'Find the wrong number' — one listed term breaks the rule the others follow.
steps: Find the rule from the terms that agree.
Point at the position that breaks it.
patterns.why: The rule fixed by the majority of terms exposes the single misfit.

revision: Routine: differences, second differences, ratios, alternating chains, position rules.
Odd gaps, square gaps, doubling gaps cover most series.
Fast growth: divide neighbours to find the multiplier.
Jumping lists: split odd and even positions.
A rule must fit every term; one misfit marks the wrong number.
Common position rules: $n^2$, $n^3$, $n^2 \pm 1$, $2^n$, $n(n+1)$, primes.

pyqPatterns.pattern: nth term or sum of an AP
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Rows of seats, monthly savings, wage steps — a quantity changes by the same amount each step, and a term or a total is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Name $a$, $d$ and $n$ from the story.
Use $a + (n-1)d$ for one term, $\frac{n}{2}[2a + (n-1)d]$ for the total.

example.q: A hall has 18 rows of chairs; the first row has 15 chairs and each row has 3 more than the previous row. How many chairs in all?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The sum of an odd number of AP terms is given, and the middle term — or a term named by its middle position — is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Middle term = sum ÷ count.
For three terms, name them a − d, a, a + d.

example.q: The sum of 15 terms of an AP is 375. Find the 8th term.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Insert k arithmetic means between a and b' — the means, their gap, or one of them is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Gap = (b − a)/(k + 1).
Build the means by adding the gap repeatedly.

example.q: Insert 4 arithmetic means between 8 and 23. Find the largest mean.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A quantity multiplies by the same factor each step (doubling, tripling) and a later term or a total is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
One term: $ar^{n-1}$.
Total: $\frac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$; if $r = 1$, the total is $na$.

example.q: Find the sum of the first 6 terms of 4, 12, 36, ...

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: An endless list with ratio between −1 and 1 (8 + 4 + 2 + ...) and its total is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Check $|r| < 1$, then use $\frac{a}{1-r}$.
Reverse use: given the sum, find $a$ or $r$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The list has unit fractions like 1/2, 1/5, 1/8 — and a term or term-number is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Flip the list into its AP.
Solve in the AP, flip the final answer back.

example.q: Which term of the HP 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, ... is 1/32?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Coefficients grow by addition while powers grow by multiplication: 1 + 2·2 + 3·4 + 4·8.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Multiply S by r, line up the powers, subtract.
Infinite case: $\frac{a}{1-r} + \frac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A run of natural numbers, squares or cubes is to be added, often starting past 1.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Apply the matching power-sum formula.
Runs that start past 1: subtract two power sums.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A chain of fractions like 1/(1·2) + 1/(2·3) + ... — the denominators overlap.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Split each term as a difference of two simple fractions.
Cancel; only the ends survive.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Next, missing or wrong term in a series
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A bare list of numbers with a '?' or 'find the wrong number' — the reasoning staple of SSC, Railway and Banking papers.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Run the routine: differences, second differences, ratios, alternating chains, position rules.
A wrong number must break the rule that fits every other term.

solvedExamples.q: A hall has 18 rows of chairs. The first row has 15 chairs and each row has 3 more chairs than the previous one. How many chairs are there in the hall?
Three numbers in GP have a sum of 21 and a product of 216. The numbers are:
solvedExamples.solution:
Name the terms $\dfrac{a}{r}, a, ar$; the product is $a^3 = 216$, so $a = 6$.
Sum: $\dfrac{6}{r} + 6 + 6r = 21 \Rightarrow 6r^2 - 15r + 6 = 0 \Rightarrow 2r^2 - 5r + 2 = 0$.
$r = 2$ (or $\dfrac{1}{2}$): the numbers are 3, 6, 12.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $a^3 = 216$ gives $a = 6$; try 3, 6, 12 — sum 21, product 216. Both check.
solvedExamples.pattern: three GP terms: sum and product

solvedExamples.q: The sum of the infinite GP $9 + 3 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{3} + \cdots$ is:
Which term of the HP $\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{5}, \dfrac{1}{8}, \ldots$ is $\dfrac{1}{32}$?
solvedExamples.shortcut: Flip to the AP: $(32 - 2) \div 3 = 10$ jumps after the first term, so the 11th term.

practice.q: Find the 10th term of the arithmetic progression 7, 11, 15, 19, ...
In an AP, the 4th term is 14 and the 9th term is 34. What is the 15th term?
What is the sum of the first 20 terms of the AP 5, 9, 13, 17, ...?
How many terms of the AP 21, 18, 15, ... must be taken so that their sum is 54?
practice.solution:
$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[42 - 3(n-1)] = 54$ gives $n^2 - 15n + 36 = 0$.
$n = 3$ or $n = 12$.
Check: $21 + 18 + 15 = 54$, and the 12-term sum (terms fall to $-12$) is also $54$.
practice.shortcut: A falling AP can pass the same total twice — test both roots.

practice.q: Which term of the AP 3, 8, 13, 18, ... is 78?
Which term of the AP $-5, -1, 3, 7, \ldots$ is 91?
practice.shortcut: Move $-5$ across first: $(91 + 5) \div 4 = 24$ jumps, so the 25th term.

practice.q: The sum of 15 terms of an AP is 375. What is its 8th term?
practice.solution:
The 8th term is the middle of 15 terms.
Middle $= \dfrac{S_{15}}{15} = \dfrac{375}{15} = 25$.

practice.q: The sum of three numbers in AP is 27 and their product is 504. The numbers are:
practice.solution:
Middle $= \dfrac{27}{3} = 9$.
Product: $9(81 - d^2) = 504 \Rightarrow d^2 = 25 \Rightarrow d = 5$.
Numbers: 4, 9, 14.
practice.shortcut: Name the terms $a-d$, $a$, $a+d$; the sum fixes $a = 9$ at once.

practice.q: Four arithmetic means are inserted between 8 and 23. The largest of these means is:
How many arithmetic means must be inserted between 5 and 35 so that the first mean is one-third of the last mean?
practice.solution:
First mean $= 5 + d$, last mean $= 35 - d$.
$5 + d = \dfrac{35 - d}{3} \Rightarrow d = 5$.
Gaps $= \dfrac{30}{5} = 6$, so means $= 6 - 1 = 5$.

practice.q: A man saves Rs 200 in the first month and increases his savings by Rs 25 every month. His total savings in 12 months (in rupees) are:
A training fee starts at Rs 800 in the first year and rises by Rs 150 every year. In which year does the total fee paid first exceed Rs 12,000?
practice.shortcut: Test years around the estimate $n \approx 9$ instead of solving a quadratic.

practice.q: In an AP, the sum of the first $p$ terms equals the sum of the first $q$ terms, where $p \ne q$. The sum of the first $(p + q)$ terms is:
practice.solution:
$S_p - S_q = (p-q)\left[a + \dfrac{(p+q-1)d}{2}\right] = 0$.
Since $p \ne q$, the bracket is 0.
$S_{p+q} = (p+q)\left[a + \dfrac{(p+q-1)d}{2}\right] = 0$.

practice.q: Find the 5th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...
The 3rd term of a GP is 12 and the 6th term is 96. The 10th term is:
What is the sum of the first 6 terms of the GP 4, 12, 36, 108, ...?
How many terms of the GP 3, 6, 12, ... must be added to get a sum of 189?
The sum of the infinite GP $8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + \cdots$ is:
The sum of an infinite GP is 27 and its first term is 18. The common ratio is:
Three numbers in GP have a sum of 35 and a product of 1000. The largest number is:
practice.solution:
Product $= a^3 = 1000$, so $a = 10$.
$\dfrac{10}{r} + 10 + 10r = 35 \Rightarrow 2r^2 - 5r + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = 2$.
Numbers: 5, 10, 20. Largest $= 20$.

practice.q: Three numbers in GP have a product of 64 and a sum of 21. The numbers are:
practice.shortcut: Option check: only 1, 4, 16 has product 64 and sum 21.

practice.q: The sum of an infinite GP is 6 and the sum of the squares of its terms is 18. The first term is:
A ball is dropped from 12 m and rebounds to half its height each time. The height of its 4th rebound (in m) is:
practice.solution:
Rebound heights form a GP: $12 \times \dfrac{1}{2}, 12 \times \dfrac{1}{4}, \ldots$
4th rebound $= 12 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 0.75$ m.

practice.q: A ball is dropped from a height of 54 m. After each bounce it rises to two-thirds of its previous height. The total distance travelled (in m) before it comes to rest is:
practice.solution:
First drop: 54 m, once.
Rebounds: $36 + 24 + 16 + \cdots = \dfrac{36}{1 - 2/3} = 108$; travelled twice.
Total $= 54 + 2 \times 108 = 270$ m.

practice.q: A man saves Rs 2 in the first month, Rs 4 in the second, Rs 8 in the third, and so on. His total savings in 10 months (in rupees) are:
A bacteria culture has 50 cells and the count doubles every hour. How many cells are there after 6 hours?
practice.solution:
Count is a GP: $a = 50$, $r = 2$.
After 6 hours: $50 \times 2^6 = 3200$.

practice.q: Which term of the HP $\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{5}, \dfrac{1}{8}, \ldots$ is $\dfrac{1}{32}$?
practice.shortcut: Flip to the AP: $(32 - 2) \div 3 = 10$ jumps after the first term, so 11th.

practice.q: The 4th term of an HP is $\dfrac{1}{10}$ and the 10th term is $\dfrac{1}{28}$. The 15th term is:
practice.solution:
Reciprocal AP: $a_4 = 10$, $a_{10} = 28$.
$6d = 18 \Rightarrow d = 3$; $a = 10 - 9 = 1$.
15th AP term $= 1 + 14 \times 3 = 43$, so the HP term is $\dfrac{1}{43}$.

practice.q: Which term of the HP $\dfrac{1}{3}, \dfrac{1}{6}, \dfrac{1}{9}, \ldots$ is $\dfrac{1}{51}$?
The 4th term of an HP is $\dfrac{1}{22}$ and the 11th term is $\dfrac{1}{43}$. The 15th term is:
practice.solution:
Reciprocal AP: $a_4 = 22$, $a_{11} = 43$.
$7d = 21 \Rightarrow d = 3$; $a = 22 - 9 = 13$.
15th AP term $= 13 + 14 \times 3 = 55$, so the HP term is $\dfrac{1}{55}$.

practice.q: The AM of two numbers is 10 and their GM is 8. Their HM is:
The AM of two positive numbers is 13 and their GM is 12. The numbers are:
practice.solution:
Sum $= 26$, product $= 144$.
$t^2 - 26t + 144 = 0$: $t = \dfrac{26 \pm 10}{2} = 18$ or $8$.
The numbers are 8 and 18.

practice.q: Find the sum $1 + 2 \times 2 + 3 \times 4 + 4 \times 8 + 5 \times 16$.
Find the sum $1 \times 2 + 2 \times 4 + 3 \times 8 + 4 \times 16 + 5 \times 32 + 6 \times 64$.
The sum of the infinite series $1 + \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{3}{9} + \dfrac{4}{27} + \cdots$ is:
The sum of the infinite series $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{2}{4} + \dfrac{3}{8} + \dfrac{4}{16} + \cdots$ is:
The reciprocals of the terms of an HP form the AP 4, 7, 10, ... The 8th term of the HP is:
practice.solution:
8th AP term $= 4 + 7 \times 3 = 25$.
So the 8th HP term is $\dfrac{1}{25}$.

practice.q: Which term of the HP $\dfrac{1}{9}, \dfrac{1}{14}, \dfrac{1}{19}, \ldots$ is $\dfrac{1}{54}$?
What is the sum $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 40$?
What is the sum $21 + 22 + 23 + \cdots + 50$?
What is the sum $1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + \cdots + 10^2$?
What is the sum $2^2 + 4^2 + 6^2 + \cdots + 20^2$?
practice.shortcut: Factor out $2^2$ first; the power sum then runs to 10, not 20.

practice.q: What is the sum $1^3 + 2^3 + \cdots + 8^3$?
What is the sum $1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + 25$?
What is the sum $11 + 13 + 15 + \cdots + 29$?
What is the sum $\dfrac{1}{1 \cdot 2} + \dfrac{1}{2 \cdot 3} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{9 \cdot 10}$?
What is the sum $\dfrac{1}{1 \cdot 5} + \dfrac{1}{5 \cdot 9} + \dfrac{1}{9 \cdot 13} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{37 \cdot 41}$?
If $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + n = 325$, then $n$ is:
What is the sum $1 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 + 3 \times 4 + \cdots + 10 \times 11$?
If $1 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 + 3 \times 4 + \cdots + n(n+1) = 168$, then $n$ is:
Find the next term: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, ...
practice.solution:
Gaps: 3, 5, 7, 9 — the odd numbers.
Next gap 11: $26 + 11 = 37$.
(The list is $n^2 + 1$: $6^2 + 1 = 37$.)

practice.q: Find the next term: 3, 4, 8, 17, 33, ...
Find the next term: 5, 10, 20, 40, ...
Find the next term: 2, 4, 12, 48, 240, ...
Find the next term: 5, 9, 7, 11, 9, 13, ...
practice.solution:
Odd positions: 5, 7, 9 ($+2$); even positions: 9, 11, 13 ($+2$).
The 7th term belongs to the odd chain: $9 + 2 = 11$.

practice.q: Find the next term: 7, 12, 10, 15, 13, 18, ...
Find the next term: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, ...
Find the next term: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ...
practice.shortcut: Gaps are 5, 7, 9, 11 — same answer either way.

practice.q: Find the missing term: 7, 14, 28, ?, 112
practice.solution:
Each term doubles.
Missing term $= 28 \times 2 = 56$ (and $56 \times 2 = 112$ checks).

practice.q: Find the missing term: 2, 3, 6, ?, 14, 15, 30
practice.solution:
The rule alternates $+1$ and $\times 2$: 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 15, 30.
Missing term $= 7$.

practice.q: Find the wrong number in the series: 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 40, 56
practice.solution:
The rule $n(n+1)$ gives 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42, 56.
The sixth term is listed as 40 — it should be 42.

practice.q: Find the wrong number in the series: 5, 11, 23, 47, 94, 191
practice.solution:
The rule $\times 2 + 1$ gives 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, 191.
The fifth term is listed as 94 — it should be 95.

practice.q: Find the next term: 2, 3, 8, 27, 112, ...
Find the next term: 1, 4, 27, 256, ...
